answer.known_results: MasakhaNER 2.0 is a named-entity recognition benchmark covering 20 African languages, including Twi, evaluated using entity-level F1. Published results show substantial variation across languages, with African-language-adapted pretrained models generally outperforming generic multilingual baselines.

MMLU tests multiple-choice knowledge across 57 subjects, including marketing, elementary mathematics, and medical genetics. Reported GPT-4 performance was about 86% accuracy, compared with roughly 44% for the largest GPT-3 model in the original evaluation.

AI2D evaluates multiple-choice question answering about school-level science diagrams. Modern vision-language models generally perform strongly on it, with leading systems reporting accuracy above 90%, substantially outperforming early baselines.

answer.benchmark_name: BIRD (BIg Bench for large-scale Database grounded text-to-SQL evaluation)
answer.known_results: The original BIRD results reported GPT-4 at roughly 54.9% execution accuracy on the test set, compared with human performance of about 92.9%. Later specialized text-to-SQL systems have substantially improved on that initial model performance.

It uses 225 Exercism coding exercises across six programming languages, scored by passing their tests. Published results show substantial differences between models, with stronger reasoning models generally doing best; scores also depend on the editing format and whether a repair attempt is allowed.

BBQ evaluates social biases in question answering using ambiguous and disambiguated contexts across nine demographic categories. Published evaluations found that language models often rely on stereotypes when contexts are ambiguous, with bias sometimes persisting even when the context supplies the answer.

answer.benchmark_name: BIRD (BIg Bench for LaRge-scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQL Evaluation)
answer.known_results: BIRD evaluates text-to-SQL on realistic databases, including external knowledge provided as evidence. Its original report found GPT-4 achieved about 54.9% execution accuracy, substantially below the reported human performance of about 92.96%.

EusTrivia is a Basque multiple-choice trivia benchmark used in evaluations of Basque language models, including Latxa, with translated versions for cross-lingual comparison. Published Latxa evaluations report strong gains over its base models and competitive performance against much larger general-purpose models on Basque tasks.

Belebele is a multilingual multiple-choice reading-comprehension benchmark covering 122 language varieties, with passages drawn from FLORES-200. Published evaluations show substantial performance gaps between high-resource and low-resource languages, with strong multilingual models still falling short of their English performance on many languages.

It is a suite of 100 prompts testing critical safety risks across five harm areas. Published evaluations found substantial variation across models, with safety-tuned systems generally performing better but some systems still producing unsafe answers to straightforward harmful prompts.

C-Eval is a Chinese multiple-choice benchmark covering 52 subjects across several educational and professional levels. Its original results reported approximately 68.7% accuracy for GPT-4 and 54.4% for ChatGPT.

CMMLU evaluates Chinese-language knowledge and reasoning across 67 subjects. Its published baseline results showed GPT-4 achieving roughly 70% accuracy and ChatGPT roughly 50%, with substantial variation across subjects.

The MATH benchmark introduced by Hendrycks et al. contains competition-style mathematics problems with worked solutions. Early language models achieved only low single-digit accuracy, while later reasoning-focused systems have achieved much higher scores, especially on the commonly used MATH-500 subset.

CRUXEval evaluates Python input prediction (CRUXEval-I) and output prediction (CRUXEval-O) on 800 short functions. Published evaluations found substantial error rates even for strong models such as GPT-4, with chain-of-thought prompting generally improving performance.

EgoSchema is a long-video question-answering benchmark built from three-minute Ego4D clips; the #C/#O narration markers are characteristic of Ego4D. Early AI systems scored roughly 30–40% on its five-choice questions, substantially below human performance of around 76%.

answer.benchmark_name: WMDP (Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy) — biology subset
answer.known_results: WMDP evaluates hazardous knowledge using multiple-choice questions in biology, chemistry, and cybersecurity. Published results show capable models scoring substantially above the 25% chance baseline, while targeted unlearning can reduce scores toward chance.

CyberGym evaluates AI agents on reproducing real-world vulnerabilities by generating proof-of-concept inputs in executable environments. Published evaluations found that even strong agents reproduce only a minority of vulnerabilities, with success depending substantially on the model, agent scaffold, and available vulnerability information.

CRAG found substantial room for improvement in retrieval-augmented question answering: even strong LLM-based systems answered fewer than two-thirds of questions correctly. Performance was particularly challenging for questions requiring temporal reasoning or combining multiple facts.

FinanceBench evaluates financial question answering grounded in public companies’ financial reports. Its published evaluation found substantial errors and refusals even among strong LLM-based systems, including retrieval-augmented configurations.

These items match BBH’s web_of_lies, causal_judgement, and object_counting tasks. The original results showed that chain-of-thought prompting substantially improved PaLM and Codex performance over direct answer-only prompting.

BBQ evaluates social biases in question answering using ambiguous and disambiguated contexts across nine social dimensions. Published evaluations found that models often rely on stereotypes when context is insufficient, with performance and bias varying by model and prompting setup.

HallusionBench evaluates visual hallucination and failures of image-context reasoning using carefully paired questions and images. Published evaluations found substantial errors even in leading vision-language models such as GPT-4V, with weaker performance on consistency-based metrics than on individual-question accuracy.

I recall AfroBench evaluating language models across many African languages and tasks, including translated knowledge and commonsense questions. Reported performance varies substantially by language, with large gaps between African-language performance and English performance.

ThaiExam evaluates language models on Thai examination questions, including school/university entrance exams and investment-consultant licensing questions. Published evaluations found GPT-4 substantially stronger than GPT-3.5 and many open-source models, with performance varying across exam categories.

At its initial release, leading AI systems generally scored below 10% accuracy. Later reasoning models and tool-assisted systems achieved substantially higher scores, with results depending on tool access and evaluation setup.

IgakuQA contains questions from Japan’s National Medical Licensing Examination. Published evaluations show GPT-4 substantially outperforming GPT-3.5, with performance varying by exam year and question format.

KMMLU is a Korean-language benchmark drawn from Korean exams across 45 subjects. Its original evaluation found that even leading models such as GPT-4 scored only around 60% accuracy, with substantial room for improvement on Korean-specific knowledge.

AlpacaEval evaluates instruction-following through pairwise judgments against reference responses, reporting win rates. Published results show substantial sensitivity to response length, motivating the length-controlled win rates used with AlpacaEval 2.0.

LegalBench evaluates legal reasoning across a broad collection of tasks, including judicial rhetorical-role classification and international citizenship law. Published evaluations generally found GPT-4 among the strongest models tested, with substantial variation in performance across tasks.

This BIG-bench task uses linguistics-exam problems to test linguistic reasoning from supplied examples. Early evaluated language models generally performed poorly relative to human solvers; I do not recall exact scores.

miniF2F is a benchmark of formalized competition-style mathematics problems, commonly evaluated by proof success rate in Lean. Published systems include GPT-f, Thor, and DeepSeek-Prover, with later theorem-proving systems achieving substantially higher success rates than early baselines.

EHRSQL evaluates text-to-SQL on electronic health records, including MIMIC-III and eICU, with unanswerable questions testing whether systems abstain appropriately. Published evaluations show that reliable abstention remains challenging, even for systems that perform well on answerable questions.

MathVista evaluates mathematical reasoning in visual contexts, including geometry diagrams and charts. Its original evaluation reported GPT-4V at about 49.9% accuracy, compared with approximately 60.3% for humans.

HEAD-QA contains multiple-choice questions from Spanish healthcare qualification exams, with Spanish and English versions. Early baseline systems performed well below human experts; later large language models achieve substantially stronger results, with performance varying by language and specialty.

MedMCQA contains four-option medical entrance-exam questions, including dental questions, primarily from Indian examinations. Original baseline systems achieved roughly 40–50% accuracy, while later strong language models have scored substantially higher.
MedQA contains USMLE-style multiple-choice medical questions. Published results include approximately 67.6% accuracy for Med-PaLM and 86.5% for Med-PaLM 2 on its USMLE evaluation.

MedQA contains USMLE-style multiple-choice medical questions, commonly evaluated using its four-option English version. GPT-4 was reported to achieve roughly 86% accuracy, substantially outperforming earlier models.

PubMedQA tests yes/no/maybe answers to biomedical research questions using PubMed abstract contexts. Published results show substantial variation across models, with strong modern language models often achieving roughly 75–85% accuracy on the expert-labeled subset.

MedHallu evaluates hallucination detection in medical question–answer pairs derived from PubMedQA. Published evaluations show that even strong language models struggle, particularly with plausible, difficult hallucinations; performance varies substantially with hallucination difficulty.

MMLU evaluates multiple-choice knowledge across 57 subjects, typically using five-shot prompts like these. The original paper reported GPT-3 at roughly 44% accuracy; later frontier models have exceeded 85%.

MMBench evaluates multimodal models using multiple-choice visual understanding questions across diverse abilities. Published evaluations generally show strong proprietary vision-language models outperforming early open-source models, with results varying by benchmark version and language.

MMLU-Pro expands and revises MMLU with harder questions and typically ten answer choices rather than four. Published initial results placed leading models roughly in the 60–75% accuracy range, substantially below their scores on the original MMLU.

These match the few-shot worked examples used in common MATH evaluation prompts. Early large language models scored in the single digits, while Minerva 540B reported approximately 50% accuracy and later reasoning models performed substantially better.

SWE-bench evaluates systems on resolving real GitHub issues by modifying repository code, with success determined by tests. The original evaluation reported low single-digit resolution rates for leading models; later coding agents achieved substantially higher scores, especially on SWE-bench Lite and Verified.

LongGenBench evaluates long-form generation with detailed constraints, including structured tasks such as city planning and skyscraper floor assignments. Reported evaluations show that even strong long-context models struggle to maintain instruction compliance and completeness as the required output grows longer.

These items are from the NAEP released-question collection, hosted by The Nation’s Report Card. I recognize the source but do not confidently recall specific published AI-system scores on this benchmark.

This benchmark contains historical CSAW CTF challenges across categories such as pwn, reverse engineering, and miscellaneous. Published evaluations show that autonomous LLM agents solve only a minority of its challenges, with performance strongly dependent on the model and agent framework.

These are from the obfuscated Blocksworld (Mystery Blocksworld) planning tasks in PlanBench. Published evaluations found that LLM planning performance dropped sharply when familiar action and predicate names were obfuscated, with early GPT-4 systems achieving near-zero success on this variant.

miniF2F is a benchmark of 488 formalized competition-level mathematics problems, with versions in proof assistants including Isabelle and Lean. Published theorem-proving systems have improved from relatively low initial pass rates to solving a majority of its test problems, though results vary substantially with the proof assistant and search budget.

The benchmark contains 939 prompts covering several categories of harmful requests. Its published evaluation found that safety-trained assistants generally handled most prompts safely, with GPT-4 among the strongest systems evaluated, though performance varied by risk category.

ASDiv is a dataset of diverse elementary-level arithmetic word problems. Published evaluations show substantial improvements from earlier math-word-problem solvers to modern language models, though I do not recall reliable model-specific scores.

GPQA contains expert-written multiple-choice questions in physics, chemistry, and biology. The original paper reported roughly 39% accuracy for GPT-4, compared with about 65% for domain experts and 34% for non-expert humans with web access.

RealTimeQA evaluates time-sensitive factual question answering using regularly collected news quizzes. Published evaluations show that retrieving up-to-date information substantially improves performance over relying on a language model's stored knowledge alone.

StatQA evaluates models’ ability to select relevant data columns and appropriate statistical methods for natural-language questions. Published evaluations show substantial room for improvement, including for strong models, particularly in selecting all applicable methods correctly.

FinBen includes a Management Assessment task evaluating qualities of executives’ earnings-call answers, such as clarity, relevance, and assertiveness. Published evaluations show substantial variation across models on this task; I do not reliably recall the exact scores.

SugarCrepe evaluates vision-language compositionality using image-caption discrimination with hard negative captions. Published results show substantial weaknesses in models such as CLIP, particularly on compositional swaps, despite strong performance on standard image-text benchmarks.

τ²-bench evaluates conversational agents in retail, airline, and telecom domains, including telecom tasks requiring coordination between agent and user actions. Published results show substantial room for improvement even for strong models, particularly on tasks requiring this coordination.

TruthfulQA tests whether models reproduce common misconceptions and false premises, using generation and multiple-choice evaluations. The original paper reported that its best tested model was truthful on about 58% of questions versus 94% for humans, and that larger models were not consistently more truthful.

τ-bench evaluates tool-using agents in simulated customer-service conversations, including airline and retail tasks, with domain policies. The original results reported GPT-4o success rates of about 35% on airline tasks and 49% on retail tasks, with substantially lower reliability when requiring repeated successful runs.

These appear to come from Self-Instruct’s user-oriented instruction evaluation set. The published evaluation found that self-instruction substantially improved GPT-3’s instruction following, although it remained behind InstructGPT.

VLRewardBench evaluates multimodal reward models and vision-language judges on paired responses, including visual reasoning and hallucination cases. Published evaluations show substantial room for improvement even for strong proprietary vision-language models, particularly on reasoning-heavy comparisons.

WorkBench evaluates agents on workplace tasks involving tools for calendar, analytics, project management, and related applications. Published evaluations show substantial gaps from reliable task completion, even for strong language-model agents.
